title: Botulinum Toxin and Injectable Filler (Aesthetic)
source_label: Pasha 6e (Reconstructive and Facial Plastic Surgery chapter)
indications: Office treatment of facial aging. Botulinum toxin treats dynamic rhytids by blocking presynaptic acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction: glabellar lines, forehead lines, lateral canthal lines (crow's feet), platysmal bands, perioral lines, mentalis dimpling, and masseter hypertrophy; it does not treat static lines or skin quality. Type A toxins (onabotulinum-, abobotulinum-, incobotulinum-, prabotulinum- and daxibotulinumtoxinA) cleave SNAP-25, while type B (rimabotulinumtoxinB) cleaves synaptobrevin (VAMP). Compared with A, type B starts working sooner but wears off sooner, stings more on injection because of its acidic pH, spreads more and causes more autonomic effects such as dry mouth, which is why it is favored for sialorrhea and for patients who no longer respond to A. Units are not interchangeable between products or serotypes. Fillers restore volume and soften static folds: hyaluronic acid (HA) for lips, nasolabial folds, tear troughs and fine lines (reversible with hyaluronidase); calcium hydroxyapatite and poly-L-lactic acid for deeper volume and lipoatrophy. Contraindications include active infection at the site, pregnancy, neuromuscular junction disorders (toxin), unrealistic expectations, and known product allergy.
setup: Consent covering bruising, asymmetry, ptosis, vascular occlusion and blindness; standardized pre-treatment photographs at rest and in animation

Reconstitute toxin per its package insert: Botox comes as freeze-dried powder in 100 U or 200 U vials (each 100 U complexed with 0.5 mg human albumin and 0.9 mg NaCl), reconstituted with preservative-free saline; draw up with a 21 g or larger needle and choose the diluent volume to set concentration (about 1.25 to 10 U per 0.1 mL), keeping injected volume small to limit spread (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 54; Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 39)

Units are product-specific mouse units and are not interchangeable between products or serotypes: about 2.5 abobotulinumtoxinA (Dysport) units per onabotulinumtoxinA (Botox) unit for facial lines, and 400 Dysport units versus 100 Botox units for pharyngoesophageal spasm; most published doses refer to Botox (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, p 516; Cummings 7e, Ch 111)
Store unopened and reconstituted vials as the package insert directs; label the vial with product, concentration and time of reconstitution, and record the lot number

Screen before injecting: pregnancy or breastfeeding, myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton syndrome or motor neuron disease, albumin hypersensitivity, and drugs that potentiate blockade (aminoglycosides, penicillamine, quinine, calcium channel blockers); counsel patients on aspirin or anticoagulants about bruising (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 54, p 1049)
30 to 32 gauge needles on tuberculin or insulin syringes; blunt cannulas (25 to 27 gauge) for deep filler planes
Topical anesthetic or ice; many HA products contain lidocaine
Vascular occlusion kit in the room: hyaluronidase (enough for repeated high doses), warm compresses, aspirin, nitroglycerin paste, emergency ophthalmology contact
Clean skin with alcohol or chlorhexidine; makeup removed
landmarks: Corrugator supercilii (belly medial, tail laterally above the brow) and procerus
Frontalis, staying about 2 cm above the brow
Lateral orbicularis oculi, about 1 cm lateral to the orbital rim
Supraorbital and supratrochlear vessels at the glabella
Angular and dorsal nasal arteries along the nose and medial canthus
Facial artery near the nasolabial fold and labial arteries deep to orbicularis oris
Superficial temporal artery in the temple
danger: Toxin diffusion into levator palpebrae causing lid ptosis (injections too low or medial at the brow or orbit); the orbital retaining ligament seal is incomplete around the supraorbital and supratrochlear bundles, giving about a 1% ptosis risk after glabellar injection (Cummings 7e, Ch 25)
Low frontalis injections causing brow ptosis
Frontalis injection after a brow lift, since frontalis is the only brow elevator
Deep orbicularis oculi injection causing lagophthalmos and exposure (Cummings 7e, Ch 26)
Perioral or depressor overtreatment causing incompetence, drooling or asymmetric smile
Deep or excessive platysmal and neck injection spreading to pharyngeal or strap muscles, causing dysphagia, aspiration and neck weakness (Cummings 7e, Ch 205)
Intra-arterial filler at the glabella, nose, nasolabial fold or temple, causing skin necrosis or retinal artery occlusion
Superficial HA in thin skin causing Tyndall (blue) discoloration
Permanent fillers producing late granulomas that cannot be dissolved
steps: Assess and plan

Separate dynamic lines (toxin) from static folds and volume loss (filler). Note pre-existing brow or lid asymmetry and ptosis, which toxin can worsen. Screen for pregnancy or lactation, myasthenia, Lambert-Eaton, aminoglycosides and anticoagulants. Agree on a conservative first dose, and document product, units, sites and photographs at every session.
Toxin: mark sites

Have the patient animate (frown, raise brows, squint) to locate hyperfunctional muscle. Mark corrugator sites at the medial belly and over the tail above the brow, a central procerus site, frontalis grid points at least 2 cm above the brow, and two to three lateral orbicularis sites at least 1 cm outside the orbital rim.
Toxin: glabella

Inject corrugator bellies deep and tails more superficially, angling upward with a finger guarding the rim, plus a central procerus point; the medial depressors typically take about 20 Botox units in total. Stay above the rim at the mid-pupillary line, because toxin can track along the supraorbital and supratrochlear bundles to the levator. Press gently after each injection.
Toxin: forehead and crow's feet

Inject frontalis in small aliquots at 3 to 5 sites per side at least 2 cm above the brow, ideally after treating the depressors, and skip frontalis after a brow lift because it is the only elevator. For crow's feet, inject superficially 1 cm outside the orbital rim, avoiding the lower canthus and the area below the zygomatic arch.
Toxin: lower face and neck

Mentalis for chin dimpling (central and low, away from orbicularis and depressor labii), tiny doses in orbicularis oris within 5 mm of the vermilion for perioral lines or lip flip (satisfaction only about 50% from enunciation and pucker problems), and platysmal bands pinched and injected superficially, never deep near strap and pharyngeal muscles where spread causes dysphagia.
Toxin: aftercare

Keep the patient upright and avoid rubbing or massage for about 6 hours to limit spread. Effect appears within a few days, peaks at 1 to 2 weeks and lasts about 3 to 4 months, until axonal sprouts form new junctions. Review at 2 weeks for touch-up; treat lid ptosis with apraclonidine drops as needed, usually for 1 to 2 weeks.
Filler: choose product and plane

Match product to depth: low-viscosity HA superficially for fine lines and lips, higher-crosslinked HA deeper for folds and cheeks, calcium hydroxyapatite or poly-L-lactic acid in deep dermal or supraperiosteal planes for volume, never in lips. Avoid permanent products for routine use.
Filler: safe injection technique

Know the arterial danger zones. Use blunt cannulas where possible in high-risk areas, inject slowly with low pressure in small aliquots, keep the needle moving or use small boluses on bone, and limit total volume per site. Aspiration is unreliable for excluding intravascular placement.
Filler: watch for blanching

Observe skin color while injecting. Immediate blanching, pain out of proportion, or a reticular dusky pattern away from the injection point indicate vascular compromise. Stop immediately; do not continue to fill the area.
Vascular occlusion response

For HA, flood the entire affected vascular territory with high-dose hyaluronidase and repeat hourly until capillary refill normalizes. Add warm compresses, massage, aspirin and topical nitroglycerin. Treat at once, since tissue salvage falls with every hour of delay, though hyaluronidase is still worth giving up to about 48 hours. Any visual change is an emergency requiring immediate ophthalmology referral.
Filler: finish

Mold gently for symmetry and smoothness, document product lot numbers, volumes and sites, and give aftercare: ice, avoid heavy exercise and pressure for 24 hours, and call immediately with pain, color change or visual symptoms.
exit_check: All injected areas well perfused with normal capillary refill; no blanching or livedo
Units, product, lot and sites documented with photographs
Patient knows warning symptoms for vascular occlusion and ptosis and how to reach the team
postop: Toxin review at 2 weeks for asymmetry and touch-up
Filler bruising and swelling settle within about 1 to 2 weeks; ice and head elevation
Nodules from HA treated with hyaluronidase; inflammatory or delayed nodules assessed for biofilm or granuloma, often with intralesional triamcinolone
Retreatment intervals: toxin about 3 to 4 months, HA 6 to 12 months or longer

early: Bruising, swelling, local pain, erythema, headache and transient hyperesthesia
Weak smile, impaired pucker or drooling after perioral or depressor overtreatment
Dysphagia or neck weakness after neck injection
Systemic symptoms (nausea, fatigue, flulike illness, distant rash) or an acute type 1 reaction
Visual loss from retinal artery embolization
late: Nodules and granulomas, especially with permanent fillers
Therapeutic failure from neutralizing antibodies with frequent high-dose toxin (rare; technique is the usual cause of failure)

attending_followup: Mechanism of botulinum toxin and duration of effect?

It cleaves SNARE proteins (type A cleaves SNAP-25) to block presynaptic acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction. Onset is 2 to 5 days, peak at 2 weeks, duration about 3 to 4 months, with recovery through axonal sprouting.
A patient has upper lid ptosis 10 days after glabellar toxin. Why and how is it treated?

Toxin diffused through the orbital septum into the levator palpebrae, usually from injections too low or medial. Treat with apraclonidine 0.5 percent eye drops, an alpha-adrenergic agonist that contracts Muller muscle to lift the lid 1 to 2 mm, until the toxin wears off.
Signs and management of filler vascular occlusion?

Immediate blanching, disproportionate pain, then dusky reticular discoloration in the territory. Stop injecting, give high-dose hyaluronidase throughout the territory repeated hourly, plus warm compresses, massage, aspirin and nitroglycerin paste. Visual symptoms mean possible ophthalmic artery embolization and need emergency ophthalmology.
Which fillers can be reversed, and what is the Tyndall effect?

Only hyaluronic acid can be dissolved, with hyaluronidase. Calcium hydroxyapatite, poly-L-lactic acid and PMMA have no reversal agent. The Tyndall effect is a bluish hue from HA placed too superficially in thin skin; treat with hyaluronidase.
Which areas carry the highest filler blindness risk?

The glabella, nasal dorsum and side wall, nasolabial fold and forehead, where branches of the ophthalmic artery (supratrochlear, supraorbital, dorsal nasal) connect with the facial and angular arteries, allowing retrograde flow to the retinal circulation.
A patient says her toxin no longer works. How do you work this up?

Check technique first: dose, dilution, product units and placement are the usual causes. True antibody-mediated resistance is rare and linked to frequent, high-dose treatment. Confirm it with an antibody assay or, more practically, a test injection into one side of the frontalis; a nonresponder to type A can be tried on type B.
Which conditions and drugs make you avoid or reduce toxin?

Pregnancy and breastfeeding; neuromuscular junction disease (myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton, motor neuron disease); albumin allergy; and drugs that add to junctional blockade, chiefly aminoglycosides, plus penicillamine, quinine and calcium channel blockers. Aspirin and anticoagulants are not absolute contraindications but increase bruising.
Why can't you swap Dysport and Botox at the same number of units?

Units are product-specific mouse-assay units. Dysport needs about 2.5 units per Botox unit for facial lines (higher ratios are used elsewhere, such as 400 versus 100 units for pharyngoesophageal spasm), spreads more, starts sooner and may last slightly longer. Always prescribe and document by product name.
